title: Text, JSON Lines and CSV on two server CPUs

plain.say: On GitHub's x86_64 and ARM64 Linux runners, Guion took less time than CPython on every text, JSON Lines and CSV lane, at 20,000 and 200,000 rows. The worst 95% upper bound of Guion's time divided by Python's was 0.976 on x86_64 and 0.859 on ARM64.
plain.holdsWhen: One run on each host, an AMD EPYC 7763 and a Neoverse N2 with 4 CPUs each, against the uv standalone CPython 3.14.7. Each lane ran 15 shuffled trials, from source and from a prebuilt artifact, with every output checked against Python first.
plain.doesntTell: Other programs or machines. On x86_64 the text margin is only 3–4%. An Intel Xeon runner measured worse on an earlier build and has not been rerun. Memory was not measured on these hosts, and the JSON Lines Python lane is the repository's data reference script, not the fastest possible Python.

plain.say: Starting from source with no compile cache, Guion finished the Richards benchmark in 28.03 ms. CPython took 64.70 ms.
plain.holdsWhen: A fresh-source run of 15 randomized trials on one Apple Silicon Mac running macOS 27, with CPython 3.14.7 and artifact format 61.
plain.doesntTell: Anything about other programs, other machines or other Python versions. On this same run Guion used more memory than Python for Richards: 23.4 MiB against 18.2 MiB. Free-threaded Python was not available to compare.

title: Three small loops after the machine-code work

plain.say: On three small loops, Guion took 0.058 s for 1,000,000 random draws against CPython's 0.282 s, 0.165 s for a 20,000,000-step integer loop against 1.593 s, and 0.031 s for 200,000 text appends against 0.057 s for the way Python programmers normally write that loop.
plain.holdsWhen: One Apple Silicon Mac, a release build of main at artifact format 61, against CPython 3.14.7, with 7 alternating runs per lane. The integer loop and the appends were checked for identical output before timing.
plain.doesntTell: Anything about real programs. These are synthetic loops, there are no confidence intervals, and the random lane compares speed only because the two generators draw different numbers. The same append statement written the slow way in Python took 4.901 s; that is Python's copy-on-every-pass pattern, not its normal style, so it is not the headline. Other machines, Linux and other Python versions were not measured.

title: Five short programs, start to finish

plain.say: Five small programs were each run from source in 21 randomized pairs against Python. Guion took 0.184 to 0.234 of Python's time on every one.
plain.holdsWhen: The same Mac and CPython 3.14.7 as the Richards run, in fresh processes, with outputs checked.
plain.doesntTell: How Guion compares on long-running or heavily optimized programs. A ratio below 1 means Guion took less time. The operating system's file cache was not controlled.

plain.say: On nine ordinary applications, timed in seven randomized pairs each, Guion's median was lower than Python's every time. The ratios run from 0.149 to 0.826.
plain.holdsWhen: The frozen application suite on one Mac with CPython 3.14.7, fresh processes, outputs checked against the expected results.
plain.doesntTell: That Guion is faster at every kind of application. The smallest gain was service health, at 0.826 of Python's time. Broader task classes and carefully matched Python implementations are still needed.

needles: Broader task classes and carefully matched Python implementations are still needed

title: Does it behave the same as Python?

plain.say: On the frozen application suite, Guion passed 127 of 127 cases and the independent Python version passed 127 of 127.
plain.holdsWhen: Current main at commit 484cefd, artifact format 61, on macOS ARM64. Every measured program output matched its expected output.
plain.doesntTell: Anything about other operating systems or CPU architectures. This checkpoint is macOS ARM64 only, and the earlier three-target cohort used an older artifact format.

title: A lockfile auditor, up to 16,384 packages

plain.say: Auditing 16,384 packages took Guion 77.71 ms and 29.7 MiB. Python took 162.23 ms and 46.7 MiB. Output was exact through 32,768 diagnostics.
plain.holdsWhen: Seven randomized fresh-process timing pairs per size, exact-output checks, Guion's source cache bypassed, one Apple Silicon host, Python 3.14.7.
plain.doesntTell: That Guion is generally faster than Python. An earlier run of this same workload was slower than Python (1.416×); a native report serializer changed that to 0.948×, and later speed-ups to 0.477×. Other programs, hosts and cold-cache runs need their own measurements.

needles: It is not evidence that Guion is generally faster than Python

title: A failing worker cancels its siblings

plain.say: When one parallel worker fails, a sibling still waiting on an HTTP response is interrupted and its connection is closed. The original failure is the one reported.
plain.holdsWhen: A local loopback test with two workers, on main at commit 484cefd, artifact format 61, macOS ARM64. The focused test passed 1/1.
plain.doesntTell: That Guion has a general async runtime, that effects already received by a remote service are rolled back, or that this holds on Linux or other targets.

needles: They do not establish a general async runtime

title: When an assistant was asked to choose

plain.say: In a frozen, independent exercise where assistants chose a language, they picked Python in all 18 choices for an older candidate. A later three-pair builder study recommended either language for two kinds of work and Guion's predecessor, Veritas, for one.
plain.holdsWhen: These are historical studies from before the current builds, and they asked a different question from the performance results above.
plain.doesntTell: Today's recommendation. Neither study is an estimate of general adoption.

title: The name, and who it honours

plain.say: Guion is named for Guion S. “Guy” Bluford Jr. On August 30, 1983, aboard Challenger on STS-8, he became the first African American to fly in space. He flew four shuttle missions and logged over 688 hours in space.
plain.holdsWhen: The naming is recorded from the project's architect. The record of his flights and career comes from NASA's biographical data and NASA's article on his first flight.
plain.doesntTell: How NASA says his name. NASA confirms he goes by “Guy”; “GUY-on” is the project's own pronunciation, not a NASA record.
